Second ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ is a letter written in chains, and it reads like a farewell. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is a prisoner in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧. He expects to die soon, and he says so plainly: the time of his departure is at hand. Most of his friends are gone. He asks for his cloak, with winter coming, and for his scrolls. Above all, he wants Timothy to come to him before winter. Of all Paul's letters, this is the last he wrote.

The listener has met ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ already: the young man from ⟦l:lystra_742|Lystra⟧, son of a Jewish mother and a Greek father, who joined ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ on his second journey and became his closest colleague. This letter adds a detail. Timothy's faith, Paul says, lived first in his grandmother ⟦p:lois_1828|Lois⟧ and his mother ⟦p:eunice_1228|Eunice⟧, and he had known the Scriptures from childhood. In the first letter Timothy was in ⟦l:ephesus_400|Ephesus⟧, facing false teachers in the church. He is there still, and some of the same troubles continue.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s own situation is very different from the one at the end of Acts. There he lived for two years in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ under guard in rented lodgings, receiving visitors freely. Here he is chained like a criminal, and a friend named ⟦p:onesiphorus_2252|Onesiphorus⟧ had to search hard to find him. He has already faced a first hearing, at which no one stood with him. Paul had been released after the imprisonment Acts describes, travelled again for a time, and was then arrested a second time, during the reign of the emperor Nero. After the great fire of Rome in the year sixty-four, Nero turned on the Christians of the city, and Paul was beheaded there not long afterwards. This letter is his final word.

The reasons for writing are both personal and urgent. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ wants ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ at his side, and asks him to bring ⟦p:mark_1679|Mark⟧, the same Mark who once deserted Paul and ⟦p:barnabas_1722|Barnabas⟧ on their first journey and caused a sharp quarrel between them, now valued and wanted. Paul also wants to hand on responsibility. The gospel has been entrusted to him, and he is passing it to Timothy, who must in turn pass it on to faithful people who will teach others. Behind this lies a darker picture: desertion in the province of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧, teachers who say the resurrection has already happened, and a time coming when people will turn away from sound teaching.

The letter moves through four short chapters. It begins with memory and encouragement, calling ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ not to be ashamed of the gospel or of ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ in prison. It goes on with images of the soldier, the athlete and the farmer, and warnings about quarrelsome teachers. It describes the hard times of the last days and points Timothy back to the Scriptures he has known since childhood. And it ends with a solemn charge, Paul's own reflection on a life nearly finished, and a list of names that brings his last circle of friends and opponents briefly into view.

This is the closing scene of ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s life as the New Testament shows it. The man who first appears in Acts as a young man at whose feet ⟦p:stephen_2802|Stephen⟧'s killers laid their cloaks now waits in ⟦l:rome_1013|Rome⟧ for his own death, still writing, still sending people out, and still asking for his parchments.

The greeting is much like the one in the first letter, but the mood is different almost at once. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ writes as a prisoner, and the opening is full of memory and longing.

He remembers his grandmother ⟦p:lois_1828|Lois⟧ and his mother ⟦p:eunice_1228|Eunice⟧, in whom this faith first lived. And he reminds Timothy of the gift he received when ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ laid hands on him, urging him to fan it into flame, because God has not given a spirit of fear.

⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ asks ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ not to be ashamed of the gospel, or of Paul himself in chains, but to share in suffering for it. He speaks of his own confidence in the one he has believed, and charges Timothy to guard the treasure entrusted to him.

The chapter ends with news, some bitter, some warm. Everyone in the province of ⟦l:asia_108|Asia⟧ has turned away from ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧, including two men named Phygelus and Hermogenes. ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ turns from those who deserted him back to ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧, and tells him to be strong. The first task is to pass on what he has learned. The teaching Timothy heard from Paul must be entrusted to faithful men who can teach others in turn. Paul, nearing his death, is thinking about the generations after him.

He then reaches for three familiar pictures of hard, single-minded work: the soldier on duty, the athlete who competes by the rules, and the farmer who labours before he eats. He reminds ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ of the gospel itself, ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus Christ⟧ raised from the dead and descended from ⟦p:david_994|David⟧, for which ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ is now chained like a criminal. The second half of the chapter returns to the troubles ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ faces. Having urged ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ to deal patiently with those who oppose him, ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ widens the view. In the last days, he says, terrible times will come, and he paints a long and dark portrait of people who love themselves, love money and love pleasure, keeping the outward form of religion but denying its power. He links them with the false teachers Timothy already knows, who work their way into households. He compares them with Jannes and Jambres, names that Jewish tradition gave to the magicians of Pharaoh who opposed ⟦p:moses_2108|Moses⟧, though the Old Testament itself does not name them.

The chapter ends by pointing ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ back to the sacred writings he has known since he was a child, the Scriptures of Israel, which ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧ describes as breathed out by God.

The final chapter opens with ⟦p:paul_2479|Paul⟧'s most solemn charge. In the presence of God and of Christ ⟦p:jesus_905|Jesus⟧, who will judge the living and the dead, he tells ⟦p:timotheus_2863|Timothy⟧ to preach the word, whether the time is convenient or not, because a time is coming when people will not put up with sound teaching.
